title: The Beginning of the End

jokes.text: Larry's therapist admits he and his wife are in bed by 10:00, which contradicts his claim to have seen Jon Stewart guest-hosting
jokes.setup: Larry tells his therapist he thinks the network is grooming Jon Stewart to replace him because he saw Jon guest-host a couple weeks ago
jokes.punchline: The therapist calmly points out Larry just said they're in bed by 10:00 most nights, so how did he see Jon Stewart? — exposing the therapist as barely paying attention while also puncturing Larry's paranoia
jokes.explanation: A beautifully dry trap — the joke works on two levels: the therapist's disengagement (he noticed a factual inconsistency rather than engaging emotionally) and Larry's paranoia being self-undermining. The structure is clean: setup planted in normal dialogue, revealed by a quiet logical catch. Character-specific: only a therapist-patient dynamic sells this. Economy is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We're in bed by 10:00 most nights.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Well, that's ok. / I can see that.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: You just said that you Don't stay up past 10:00. So I didn't know how You had seen Jon Stewart.

jokes.text: Larry asks his therapist, 'Could we just look at this again?' and the therapist immediately ends the session: 'Why don't we just stop it here, and I'll see ya next week.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to re-examine his contradiction about Jon Stewart; he's in a vulnerable, introspective place
jokes.punchline: The therapist cuts him off and ends the session the moment things get complicated, revealing him as completely checked-out
jokes.explanation: The therapist-as-disengaged-hack is a well-worn trope, but it lands here because the dismissal comes right after the Jon Stewart catch. The juxtaposition of Larry's emotional need versus the therapist's mechanical exit is sharp in context. Not original enough to score higher, but well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: How goes The head doctor?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What's not to like? I got a lollipop, And he shaved me Before the exam.

jokes.text: Artie: 'What's not to like? I got a lollipop, and he shaved me before the exam.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks Larry how the head doctor went
jokes.punchline: Artie responds as if a visit to a therapist is identical to a physical exam, describing receiving a lollipop and being shaved — possibly true, possibly Artie being absurdist, either way deeply in character
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Artie — gruff, oblique, and weirdly specific. 'He shaved me before the exam' is a perfect Rip Torn non-sequitur delivered with total confidence. The joke says everything about Artie's character: he doesn't understand or doesn't care about the concept of therapy, and treats all doctors the same. Highly quotable, very character-specific, economical. High craft total because the character integration is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: First of all, There should be A law on the book That prevents Network people From using The word 'creative' In their job titles. They see it On their stationery And they start Believing it.

jokes.text: Artie tells Larry about 'Kenny fucking Mitchell' being assigned as creative consultant, then: 'First of all, there should be a law on the book that prevents network people from using the word creative in their job titles. They see it on their stationery and they start believing it.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers the bad news that the network has assigned a 'creative consultant' to the show
jokes.punchline: Artie's rant that 'creative' on a network title is a dangerous fiction — they see it on stationery and start believing it
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry satire delivered in Artie's voice with real bite. The 'stationery' detail elevates this from a generic network-exec insult into something specific and visual — you can picture a suit reading his own business card and getting ideas. Character-appropriate indignation from Artie, who represents the old guard. Solid craft.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I'm his interpreter. I speak fluent bullshit.'
jokes.setup: Stevie the agent is on the phone talking in agent-speak, and Larry is struggling with the empty platitudes
jokes.punchline: Artie introduces himself as an interpreter who speaks 'fluent bullshit'
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — four words ('I speak fluent bullshit') do all the work. The setup is natural (Stevie is clearly spinning on the phone) and the punchline is perfectly timed and quotable. Slightly undercut by the concept not being fully novel (the 'translator for B.S.' idea exists elsewhere), but the execution is crisp and Artie-specific.

jokes.text: Stevie, while on his cell phone doing business, shouts 'Get out of the way, you stupid chink bitch!' at a driver mid-conversation about how great negotiations are going
jokes.setup: Stevie is performing his professional patter — 'the ball's in their court,' everything's great — while driving on Melrose
jokes.punchline: The mask slips completely as he screams a racial slur at another driver, exposing the real person beneath the agent performance
jokes.explanation: Functionally effective as character revelation — Stevie's veneer drops instantly — and the tonal whiplash (from smooth agent talk to road-rage slur) is structurally sound. However, it relies on a slur for shock, which is a cheap shortcut even by late-90s HBO standards. The earned-vs-cheap score reflects this. It works contextually but isn't clever writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That's the trouble With hollywood, Larry. Everyone's got two pricks And three assholes. It's a genitalia Horn of plenty.

jokes.text: Larry asks 'What canyon comes off Melrose?' and Artie deadpans: 'Bullshit Canyon, that's what.'
jokes.setup: Stevie has just conveniently 'lost signal' after being caught in his bullshit; Larry asks literally what canyon is off Melrose
jokes.punchline: Artie names the fictional canyon — 'Bullshit Canyon' — with total conviction, as if it's a real place
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally economical. The literal/metaphorical double-meaning of 'Bullshit Canyon' is perfectly constructed: it answers Larry's straight question (what canyon?) while summarizing Stevie's entire professional practice. Artie delivering it as geographic fact — zero ironic wink — makes it land harder. The callback to 'fluent bullshit' deepens it. This is close to an 8 anchor: sharp, character-specific, quotable, zero wasted words.

jokes.text: Artie: 'That's the trouble with Hollywood, Larry. Everyone's got two pricks and three assholes. It's a genitalia horn of plenty.'
jokes.setup: Discussion of whether Stevie the agent can be 'a nice guy' — Larry defending him, Artie skeptical
jokes.punchline: Artie summarizes Hollywood's moral anatomy as a 'genitalia horn of plenty' — too many pricks and assholes to count
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Genitalia horn of plenty' is a genuinely original construction — the Thanksgiving/abundance imagery mashed with crude anatomy is unexpected and inspired. Only Artie could say this with utter seriousness. It's got structure (setup in the prick/asshole arithmetic, punchline in the 'horn of plenty' naming), it's highly quotable, and it says something true about Hollywood. Justifies the 8+ craft score by matching the quality of the anchor examples — it's that unexpected and specific.

jokes.text: Larry reads fan mail: 'Dear sir, your show is technically crippling. What's left of humanity? Love, Ted K.' and Artie says 'This must be for Hank.'
jokes.setup: Larry wonders why his fan mail handwriting matches the Unabomber's; he reads a letter signed 'Ted K.'
jokes.punchline: Artie's deadpan: 'This must be for Hank' — implying the Unabomber is a Hank fan, not a Larry fan, and that Hank deserves the contempt
jokes.explanation: Dark, efficient, and specific to the show's internal hierarchy. The Unabomber reference is a product of its era (mid-90s) but still lands. The punchline redirecting it to Hank is the real joke — a casual, devastating demotion of Hank's audience. Three words do the work. Loses some points for relying on a topical reference that dates it.

dialogue.speaker: Kenny

jokes.text: Kenny announces the show is beating Letterman in Indianapolis — 'His own backyard.' Artie: 'Let's all join the fucking circus.'
jokes.setup: Kenny is breathlessly excited that the show is up .32 in 18-35s and beating Letterman in Indianapolis, calling it Letterman's 'own backyard'
jokes.punchline: Artie deflates the entire celebration with one line — 'Let's all join the fucking circus' — and implicitly, the audience knows Indianapolis is not Letterman's backyard (he's from there but it's irrelevant)
jokes.explanation: Artie as permanent deflator is his core function, and this is a good instance. 'His own backyard' is a stretch from Kenny that earns mockery, and 'Let's all join the fucking circus' is proportionally contemptuous. Solid but not exceptional — the joke type (mocking network enthusiasm) is familiar territory for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Let's all join The fucking circus.

jokes.text: On the proposed removal of Larry's desk: 'This desk is the most lasting relationship that Larry's ever had. He's married to this desk. It's there for him every night, and it allows him to come in from the rear.'
jokes.setup: Kenny suggests removing Larry's desk because research says it'll make Larry more accessible
jokes.punchline: Artie defends the desk by describing it as Larry's most stable relationship — then lands a double-entendre about the desk allowing Larry to 'come in from the rear'
jokes.explanation: The sequence builds well: 'most lasting relationship' → 'married to this desk' → 'there for him every night' are all darkly true character observations about Larry's emotional unavailability, and they build naturally to the rear-entry double-entendre. The joke works on both the crude and the character level simultaneously — you can laugh at the sex joke AND the sad truth about Larry. That layering earns the high score.

dialogue.speaker: Kenny
dialogue.line: We're beating Letterman In indianapolis. His own backyard.

jokes.text: Regarding the guest lineup of Scorsese, Reiser, and Colin Hay — Kenny: 'Where's the sex?' Artie: 'On Keenan?'
jokes.setup: Kenny looks at the guest lineup and asks where the sex appeal is
jokes.punchline: Artie's deadpan redirect to Keenan's show — implying their competition has sex appeal, or sarcastically suggesting they look there for it
jokes.explanation: A quick, dry volley that works in the rhythm of the scene. The 'Keenan' reference is a specific contemporary jab (Keenan Ivory Wayans had a late-night show at the time), which gives it insider flavor. But it's a minor beat — quick and functional rather than developed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie

jokes.text: Artie's suggestion for getting a Hugh Grant-type booking: 'We'll have our bookers scour Sunset after midnight, and the first celeb we find getting blown by a hooker, consider him booked. Or her.'
jokes.setup: Kenny wants to dump Scorsese for a Hugh Grant — implicitly referencing Hugh Grant's 1995 prostitution arrest
jokes.punchline: Artie takes the Hugh Grant reference literally and suggests actively finding celebrities in compromising situations as a booking strategy — then adds 'Or her' as a gender-inclusive afterthought
jokes.explanation: Brilliant industry satire with a perfect structure. Artie literalizes the subtext of celebrity scandal booking (shows DO rush to book people in the news) and presents it as a logical business plan — then 'Or her' is a pitch-perfect deadpan kicker. The joke works as media criticism, character comedy (only Artie would say this with such professional detachment), and dark comedy simultaneously. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft and higher in impact.

jokes.text: Artie exits past Kenny, pausing to say: 'I thought we sprayed for roaches last week.'
jokes.setup: Artie is done with Kenny and exits
jokes.punchline: The roach metaphor for Kenny — delivered as a casual maintenance observation, not an insult
jokes.explanation: Artie's exit line is perfectly calibrated — the insult is so understated it almost reads as genuine confusion. 'We sprayed for roaches' implies Kenny is vermin without ever saying it directly. Maximum economy, complete character integration (Artie would never do a direct insult when an oblique one is available). Loses points for originality since pest=person is a familiar metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Artie

jokes.text: Hank's new position on the set — being moved progressively further from the desk until he's essentially next to the band, physically demonstrating his marginalization
jokes.setup: Kenny tells Hank he's been moved to a 'special area' — Hank sits in one chair, Kenny says 'further,' Hank moves again, can't go further
jokes.punchline: The physical staging makes Hank's professional diminishment literal — he's been physically exiled to the edge of his own show
jokes.explanation: A primarily visual joke that lands hard in context. The escalating 'further... further... can't go any further' is a perfect comedic escalation — each beat amplifies the indignity. Hank's physical expulsion from the show mirrors his professional precarity, and the visual staging is the kind of sustained cringe Larry Sanders does best. High craft because the joke is structurally complete and emotionally resonant.

jokes.setup: Hank has walked as far as he can go toward the band.
jokes.punchline: Kenny's spin on the absurd placement — 'It's fresher' — is a perfect corporate non-answer that doubles down on the humiliation.
jokes.explanation: The button on the physical relocation gag. 'It's fresher' is a wonderful piece of corporate spin — meaningless but delivered with confidence. Works as the punchline to the extended visual escalation.

jokes.text: Hank invents a medical condition to avoid sitting near the band: 'I have a severe hearing disorder... a punctured eardrum... whenever I'm near a loud noise such as a band, my head feels like it's just... [groans] I mean, have you seen the Zapruder film?'
jokes.setup: Hank is desperate to avoid being placed next to the band; he fabricates a medical condition
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'hearing disorder' → 'punctured eardrum' → 'Zapruder film' — invoking JFK assassination footage to describe what being near the band does to his head
jokes.explanation: Jeffrey Tambor's Hank is at his cringing best here. The escalation of the fake diagnosis is perfectly structured, and 'Have you seen the Zapruder film?' as the culminating metaphor for his head-exploding distress is genuinely inspired — dark, specific, unexpected, and totally in character for someone who is both desperate and oblivious enough to make this comparison out loud. The joke earns its 8+ by being Hank-specific (nobody else on the show could deliver this) and by the originality of the Zapruder reference.

jokes.text: Artie vs. Kenny backstage confrontation: 'Are you a moron?' / 'Why don't you get off my ass?' / 'Why don't you get off my stage like you promised?' / 'Hey, say it now, Arthur, because pretty soon you won't be able to say it at all. Your show's on its last legs.' / 'No kidding? Yep.' / '[Yelling]'
jokes.setup: Artie catches Kenny backstage 30 minutes before showtime violating their agreement; they argue over a monologue note
jokes.punchline: The confrontation escalates to open hostility with Kenny predicting the show's demise as a 'tired little piece-of-shit stepping stone' for him — Artie's yell is the response
jokes.explanation: A tense, funny scene that earns its comedy from the power dynamics more than any single line. Kenny's 'tired little piece-of-shit stepping stone' is cruel and specific, and Artie's barely contained rage is the comedic engine. Not the sharpest exchange in the episode but effectively cringe-inducing.

jokes.text: The meeting upstairs — Stevie's negotiation tactic: 'How many guys are gonna come in here and blow me?' — then listing demands while the network counters with Jon Stewart's cheaper numbers
jokes.setup: Stevie is supposedly negotiating hard for Larry while simultaneously representing Jon Stewart
jokes.punchline: 'How many guys are gonna come in here and blow me?' — Stevie's crude protest is meant to sound tough but reveals he has no leverage
jokes.explanation: Stevie's crude bravado is consistent character work but the joke itself is fairly stock — the agent who talks tough but has no cards. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Do I look deaf to you? 'Cause you're talking to me like I'm deaf. Do deaf people walk around in $3,000 suits? I don't think so!'
jokes.setup: The network exec is repeating that Jon Stewart matches or beats Larry's numbers; Stevie protests being talked down to
jokes.punchline: The logic that $3,000 suits and deafness are mutually exclusive — a non-sequitur that reveals Stevie's mind working in pure status terms
jokes.explanation: The absurd non-sequitur logic ('deaf people don't wear $3,000 suits') is a funny window into Stevie's worldview where material success and sensory capacity are linked. It's a brief but effective character beat — the joke is that Stevie genuinely believes this counts as an argument.

jokes.text: Network exec reveals Stevie is also negotiating deals for Michael Richards and Jon Lovitz — Stevie: 'Yes, I am!'
jokes.setup: Stevie threatens to 'shop Larry' if they don't get an offer they like — putting on maximum bravado
jokes.punchline: The exec reveals Stevie's negotiating leverage is undermined by the fact that he's also negotiating deals with the same network for two other clients — Stevie defiantly confirms it, not seeing the problem
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — Stevie's bluster is deflated by evidence of his own conflicts of interest, and his proud 'Yes, I am!' is the perfect clueless response. The rhythm of revelation-and-response is crisp.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart scene: Stevie tells Jon that Larry 'turned him on' to Stewart and 'He's cool with this' — a beat after reassuring Jon that Larry is fine with him potentially taking over Larry's show
jokes.setup: Jon Stewart expresses discomfort about the ethics of taking over Larry's show while Larry is still negotiating; Stevie smoothly reassures him
jokes.punchline: Stevie's assurance is obviously false — everything we've seen shows Larry is not 'cool with this' — and the ease with which Stevie lies makes it both funny and uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: The irony of Stevie's reassurance is the joke — we know he's lying, Stewart half-knows he's lying, but the social machinery of Hollywood keeps it going. Effective cringe but more of a plot beat than a fully crafted comedic moment.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart's agent/manager meeting: 'They took the veal off the menu. I hate this fucking place.' — the scene cuts to a power lunch where a minor menu complaint is the first thing out of anyone's mouth
jokes.setup: Cut to a fancy restaurant where Jon Stewart is being courted to take over Larry's show. The first line is a complaint about veal.
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of high-stakes career scheming with petty menu grievances captures Hollywood power-lunch culture perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Nice scene-setting gag — the veal complaint as opening line immediately establishes the tone of this world. But it's more observed detail than a developed joke. Works as tone-setting rather than a standalone comedic beat.

jokes.text: Hank to his doctor: 'Jesus Christ, my rectal tract paid for your Jaguar.'
jokes.setup: Hank is arguing with his doctor, apparently trying to get a medical note excusing him from sitting near the band
jokes.punchline: Hank invokes his rectal history as currency — implying he's been such a frequent/profitable patient (specifically for rectal issues) that he deserves this favor
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'My rectal tract paid for your Jaguar' is an astonishing construction — it simultaneously reveals Hank's medical history (rectal problems, apparently extensive and expensive), his sense of entitlement, his transactional view of all relationships, and his complete lack of self-awareness about what he's revealing. The specificity of 'Jaguar' (not just 'car') is perfect. This is genuinely exceptional writing — specific, character-integrated, economical, original. Comparable in quality to the Snip/Snap anchor though less iconic.

jokes.text: Artie pours Hank a drink and says 'Let's drink first' before delivering bad news — Hank immediately catastrophizes: 'I knew I was on my way out. This move to the band is like getting on the fucking bus to Auschwitz.'
jokes.setup: Artie says he has bad news and wants to drink first
jokes.punchline: Hank leaps immediately to the worst possible conclusion, comparing his new seating position to Holocaust deportation — which is both monstrous and perfectly Hank
jokes.explanation: Hank's Holocaust comparison for his seating relocation is grotesque and hilarious — it's the exact kind of self-absorbed celebrity thinking that makes Hank one of TV's great comic characters. The 'bus to Auschwitz' line is dark enough to shock but delivered with such genuine distress that it works as character comedy rather than cheap shock. High character integration because only Hank's particular brand of solipsism and drama produces this.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Jesus christ, my rectal tract Paid for your jaguar.

jokes.text: Hank's immediate, correct guess: 'Oh my god. I knew I was on my way out. This move to the band is like getting on the fucking bus to Auschwitz. I'm on my way out.'
jokes.setup: Artie says he has bad news and wants to drink first. Hank immediately catastrophizes.
jokes.punchline: Hank's Holocaust comparison for being moved a few feet from the desk on a talk show set is the joke — a perfectly calibrated example of his self-dramatizing narcissism.
jokes.explanation: The Auschwitz comparison is a classic Hank move — reaching for the most extreme possible historical atrocity to describe a minor professional setback. It's dark, it's wrong, and it's perfectly in character for a man who sees himself as the center of the universe. The repetition of 'I'm on my way out' after each escalation adds to the comedic rhythm.

dialogue.line: This move to the band Is like getting on The fucking bus To auschwitz. I'm on my way out.

jokes.text: Artie reveals the bad news isn't about Hank — it's about Larry. Hank: 'I'm in. You're out.' [Laughs] 'Boy, oh, boy.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been spiraling about being on his way out; the bad news turns out to be about Larry, not Hank
jokes.punchline: Hank's immediate pivot from existential despair to gleeful relief — 'I'm in. You're out' — reveals his narcissism with devastating efficiency. He laughs at his friend's professional demise.
jokes.explanation: The reversal is structurally perfect: Hank's spiral of self-pity about being 'on the bus to Auschwitz' collapses the instant he learns the news is about Larry, replaced by immediate, undisguised glee. 'I'm in. You're out.' as a five-word response to a friend's career ending is one of the episode's sharpest character moments. The callback to his earlier catastrophizing makes the pivot funnier. Earns high craft because it requires everything that came before to land — it's integrated comedy, not a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Stevie arrives late to the production meeting. Asked which client the Entertainment Weekly shoot was for — 'No, it was for me. It was for Entertainment Weekly, the 50 Most Powerful People in Hollywood Under 30.' Larry: 'I thought you were 32.' Stevie: 'Yeah... well... Congratulations.' Larry: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Stevie arrives late from a photo shoot; everyone assumes it's for a client
jokes.punchline: It was for Stevie himself — and he's 32, not under 30. The exchange where Stevie awkwardly pivots to 'Congratulations' and Larry takes it at face value is beautifully dry.
jokes.explanation: Sharply constructed: the vanity of the agent (photo shoot for himself), the absurdity of the age lie (32 is not under 30), and then the social awkwardness of Stevie just saying 'Congratulations' as a pivot — which Larry accepts without comment. The deadpan acceptance is the real punchline. Very much in the show's register of letting characters embarrass themselves without calling it out.

jokes.text: Larry confronts Stevie about representing Jon Stewart — Stevie: 'Hey, that's what life is about, Larry. It's about conflict. Yeah, you have to learn to balance things out... and I think I do a pretty good fucking job.'
jokes.setup: Larry points out that Stevie representing his potential replacement is 'a tad of a conflict' of interest
jokes.punchline: Stevie reframes representing both sides of a negotiation as a life philosophy about 'balance' — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Stevie's self-justifying logic is good character comedy. The irony that 'conflict' is his word for conflict-of-interest is subtle and nice. Not exceptional but solid.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I remember you Tooting up behind a tree, Using your cell phone.

jokes.text: Artie confronts Stevie at the show entrance: 'Larry trusted you, you fucking goddamn lowlife.' Stevie: 'Hey, I love Larry, ok? I was at his mother's funeral. Remember?' Artie: 'I remember you tooting up behind a tree, using your cell phone.'
jokes.setup: Artie physically accosts Stevie and accuses him of betraying Larry; Stevie defends himself by invoking his presence at Larry's mother's funeral
jokes.punchline: Artie's memory of that funeral is that Stevie was doing cocaine behind a tree while on his cell phone — which is somehow worse than not attending
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. Stevie's defense ('I was at his mother's funeral') is meant to establish emotional loyalty — and Artie's counter-memory is a perfect deflation: being at a funeral while doing coke behind a tree is arguably worse than absence. 'Tooting up' is a great period-specific word choice. The image is vivid, specific, and devastating. This is the kind of detail that separates great TV writing from average — it tells you everything about Stevie in one sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, we're all A little nervous here At the Larry Sanders show Because the network Is requiring us To attend a sexual Harassment seminar On friday, And I still Don't have a date.

jokes.text: Larry at the show's monologue: 'Well, we're all a little nervous here at the Larry Sanders Show because the network is requiring us to attend a sexual harassment seminar on Friday... and I still don't have a date.'
jokes.setup: Larry introduces the sexual harassment seminar topic, framing it as something making the staff nervous
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'nervous about sexual harassment' to 'I still don't have a date' — treating the seminar as a social event and himself as lonely
jokes.explanation: A solid on-air joke with good misdirection — 'nervous' sets up anxiety about the seminar, the punchline reframes it as social anxiety about attending alone. Clean structure, works as both a Larry monologue joke and as meta-commentary on Larry's loneliness. The studio audience's laughter confirms it lands.

dialogue.line: That's what makes it A great company.
Country.

jokes.text: Kenny says 'That's what America is all about, ok? That's what makes it a great company.' Larry corrects him: 'Country.' Kenny: 'What did I say?'
jokes.setup: Kenny is mid-rant about exercising his right to be the best he can be in America
jokes.punchline: Kenny accidentally calls America a 'company' instead of a 'country' — revealing he's so corporate-brained that nation and corporation have merged in his mind — then asks 'What did I say?' as if genuinely unsure
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in character-specific wordplay. Kenny calling America a 'company' is the perfect Freudian slip for a network executive whose entire worldview is corporate. 'What did I say?' confirms he's not even aware of the distinction. Two words of setup, two words of correction, four words of clueless response — maximum economy, maximum character revelation. This earns its 8+ because it's a tiny joke that perfectly X-rays a character.

jokes.text: Larry's chicken flu monologue joke: 'The chicken flu is really something. Boy, oh, boy, my chicken has been in bed for 6 weeks.' [pause] 'I really just hope my cock doesn't get it.'
jokes.setup: Larry talks about the chicken flu epidemic on the monologue
jokes.punchline: The word 'cock' as a synonym for rooster — but landing as a sexual double-entendre — with the pause before it being the structural key
jokes.explanation: A functional double-entendre — 'cock' as rooster/penis is an old joke structure, but it works in the context of a late-night monologue and the studio audience responds. The pause before the punchline is the real craft here. Below the show's usual standard for originality but competently executed.

jokes.text: Larry sits in the new deskless set — long pause — audience chuckles at his visible discomfort as he sits exposed without his usual desk shield
jokes.setup: Larry has moved to the new deskless set as recommended by Kenny's research; he introduces it to the audience
jokes.punchline: The long, exposed pause as Larry sits there with nothing in front of him — the audience laughs at his naked vulnerability, which mirrors his actual emotional state in the episode
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most formally sophisticated comedic moment — a visual joke that is also thematic payoff. The desk has been established as Larry's emotional armor ('this desk is the most lasting relationship Larry's ever had'). Removing it and making him sit in silence is the joke AND the episode's central metaphor made literal. The audience laugh at [14:21] confirms it lands. High craft despite zero quotability because it's entirely visual/structural comedy. The rewatch bonus is high: on second viewing, knowing what the desk means, the silence hits harder.

jokes.punchline: He claims viewers have been requesting to see his lap — a transparently absurd rationalization delivered with false confidence
jokes.explanation: Larry's attempt to spin the desk removal as fan service is delightfully pathetic — 'a lot of letters asking to see my lap' is obviously invented, and the flat delivery of 'here it is' sells his internal humiliation. Good character comedy in the show's register.

jokes.explanation: The relocation joke goes live, and Larry's professional instinct to turn awkwardness into comedy ('do we have a beeper for Hank?') is both funny and revealing — even on his worst night, Larry can work a room. The rimshot on the beeper line is perfect punctuation. Strong callback payoff.

jokes.explanation: Hank trying to sound knowing and hip with 'Downtown' and then immediately hollowing it out by asking which city is a precise character beat — his performative confidence dissolving in real time. The audience laugh confirms it. Good Hank writing.

jokes.punchline: Artie's suggestion: a body pillow to hump when nervous — delivered as a practical production suggestion
jokes.explanation: Crude but character-specific — Artie's comfort solution is both ridiculous and pitched as perfectly reasonable. The delivery ('so if you get nervous, you can start humping one of them') lands as Artie's deadpan practicality rather than a crude joke. Solid but not the episode's best.

jokes.text: Colin Hay's interview: Larry says his label is called 'Lazy Eye Records' — Colin says 'Right, because, uh... because I have one?' — Larry awkwardly confirms: 'No! It's not that at all, but that's a very interesting thing you mentioned there... that I do have a lazy eye.'
jokes.setup: Colin Hay mentions his record label is called 'Lazy Eye Records'
jokes.punchline: Larry assumes it's named after Colin Hay's actual lazy eye (which he has), Colin tries to correct him, but Larry has already committed — then describes the eye as having 'a blatant disrespect for me and for anything that I look at'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most sustained cringe sequences, and it's beautifully executed. Larry walks into the label name, assumes it's about the eye, is corrected, but then describes the eye anyway — and Colin Hay's 'I wish I could look away' is a perfect kicker. The description of the lazy eye as having 'a blatant disrespect for me and for anything that I look at' is inspired — funny, specific, and delivered with Larry's awkward earnestness. Colin Hay playing it real (he actually has a lazy eye) makes the cringe authentic. This is the show at its best.

jokes.text: Colin Hay to Larry: 'Look how uncomfortable I am.' Larry: 'Yeah, well, it's gonna take some getting used to. I used to have a desk myself. I don't know who I am anymore.' Colin: 'You're Larry Sanders.' Larry: 'Well, who is that? Just someone who does whatever the network tells him to do?'
jokes.setup: Colin Hay comments on his discomfort in the new set without a desk
jokes.punchline: Larry's existential 'I don't know who I am anymore' gets a straight answer from Colin — 'You're Larry Sanders' — and Larry rejects even that as sufficient identity, spiraling into 'who is that?'
jokes.explanation: This is a great scene that lives at the border of comedy and pathos — which is where Larry Sanders always operates best. 'I don't know who I am anymore' played for laughs but also genuinely meaning it. Colin Hay's simple 'You're Larry Sanders' answered by Larry's 'Well, who is that?' is simultaneously funny and devastating. On-air vulnerability disguised as existential comedy. High character integration because no other character on any other show could have this exchange.

jokes.text: Colin Hay tells Larry mid-interview that he wrote a screenplay he thinks would be 'fantastic for Patrick Swayze' and asks if Larry can help get it to him
jokes.setup: Larry has just asked Colin to make him feel better about his identity crisis
jokes.punchline: Colin's response to Larry's emotional vulnerability is to immediately pitch his Patrick Swayze screenplay — a perfect Hollywood non-sequitur that exposes everyone as networking even in moments of apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfect showbiz satire — the moment Larry opens up ('I was hoping maybe you could make me feel a little better'), Colin's response is to pitch a screenplay. The gap between emotional register (Larry's vulnerability) and Colin's response (pure networking) is the joke. And asking for help getting it to Patrick Swayze specifically — a very specific, slightly faded star — is exactly the right detail. Larry's silence followed by 'Is my time just about up?' is the kicker.

jokes.punchline: Larry checks if the interview segment is over — using the talk show formula as an escape hatch from the absurd situation
jokes.explanation: The perfect escape-hatch line — Larry retreating into the format of his show to end an awkward moment. Maximum economy. The joke is in what he doesn't say: he's not going to help with the screenplay, and he's done with this interview. The talk show structure used as social cover.

jokes.setup: Larry asks Kenny if he can have the desk back; Kenny says it's 'coming from upstairs'
jokes.punchline: Larry's slow comprehension that Kenny is lying — 'I just asked you' / long pause / 'Oh. I get it' — is a perfectly timed realization beat
jokes.explanation: The timing is the joke — 'How could it be coming from upstairs? I just asked you' is the logical setup, then the long pause while Larry processes the absurdity, then 'Oh. I get it' — he's been lied to in the most transparent possible way. The whisper and the footsteps completing the scene make it a perfect, economical moment of sad clarity.

jokes.text: Artie and Larry look at each other after the Kenny exchange — Larry: 'What a fucking business.' Artie: 'Yeah.' Larry: 'They think it's about a desk.' Artie: 'Yeah. That's right.' Larry: 'What do you do about it?' [Long pause] Artie: 'You put your foot down.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just realized Kenny was lying; he and Artie share a moment of industry disillusionment
jokes.punchline: Artie's advice — 'You put your foot down' — delivered with great authority after a long pause, setting up what Larry does next
jokes.explanation: Works as setup for the episode's climax — Artie's advice is genuine but will be catastrophically misapplied. The deliberate pacing, the weight of the pause, and Artie's conviction make it both funny and portentous. The comedy is in the gap between how Artie means it and how Larry will execute it.

Larry: 'What do you do about it?' Long pause. Artie: 'You put your foot down.' Silence. Larry: 'Right.' Silence. Larry: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie have a post-show debrief in the empty studio, processing the desk removal and broader career crisis
jokes.punchline: Artie's advice is 'put your foot down' — delivered in a way that implies immediate action — but then nothing happens. Two beats of silence. 'Thank you.'
jokes.explanation: A scene that functions as both comedy and drama. The silences ARE the joke — Artie tells Larry to put his foot down, Larry absorbs this, says nothing for a beat, then thanks him as if he's been given actionable wisdom. The humor comes from the gap between the gravitas of the advice and the certainty that Larry will do nothing. The economy here is exceptional — the laughs are entirely in what isn't said. Great use of the awkward pause as a comedic tool.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're fired.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air announcement that he will not be coming back when his contract is up in 8 weeks — spontaneous, unplanned — while Artie backstage: 'What the fuck was that?' Stevie: 'Shit, I swear I had no idea about this.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been advised to 'put his foot down'; Kenny won't give him the desk back; everything in his professional life is collapsing
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'foot down' is to announce on live television that he's leaving — to Artie and Stevie's complete horror backstage — with 'No flipping' as his coda
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic and dramatic climax, and it earns both. The entire episode builds to this: Larry's paranoia, the contract negotiations, Kenny's manipulations, the desk removal, Artie's advice — all converging in Larry doing the most Larry thing possible: making an enormous, career-defining decision live on air out of wounded pride and insecurity. The backstage reaction ('What the fuck was that?') is the punchline. 'No flipping' as his final instruction — the host's control freak detail even in career implosion — is perfect character specificity. This justifies 8.5+ craft because it's not just a joke, it's the structural payoff of the entire episode delivered as comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're fired.

jokes.text: Artie's post-show checklist to diagnose Larry's impulsive announcement: 'I have to run down the checklist just to be sure. You on any medication? No. Just break up with someone? No.' Larry: 'I would like the desk back for the last 8 weeks.' Artie: 'You're fired.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to understand why Larry made the announcement; Larry's explanation for what provoked it is: he wants the desk back
jokes.punchline: 'You're fired.' — Artie's response to learning the desk was the triggering issue. Then a beat, followed by Artie walking it back.
jokes.explanation: The desk callback lands its final blow here — after all the negotiation, the network politics, the Jon Stewart anxiety, the reason Larry blew up his career on live television was the desk. Artie's checklist is wonderfully precise character comedy (did you break up with someone? take medication?) and 'You're fired' as the response to 'I want the desk back' is perfectly calibrated. The pause between 'You're fired' and Artie's reassurance escalates and then deflates beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: When I said Put your foot down, I think you Misunderstood me.

jokes.text: Artie's final line: 'When I said put your foot down, I think you misunderstood me.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just burned down his show by announcing his departure on live TV; Artie is trying to process it
jokes.punchline: Artie's understatement — 'I think you misunderstood me' — for an act of self-destruction that cost Larry everything, delivered in Artie's driest possible register
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing line, and it's near-perfect. The entire episode's comedy and drama resolves in nine words: 'When I said put your foot down, I think you misunderstood me.' The understatement is total — 'misunderstood' for 'ended your career on live television.' The economy is flawless. It only works because of everything that came before (making it the episode's purest callback), and it ends on Artie's voice — the show's moral and comedic center. This is how great sitcom writing closes — with a quiet line that contains everything. Just below the 'genitalia horn of plenty' in quotability but superior in structural function.

tmdb_overview: Kenny Mitchell joins the show as creative consultant and makes major changes to the format. Larry battles with the network and his agent over his contract.
